correctness.rationale: For \(p\ge2\), coordinatewise orthogonal copies of the input give a unit witness with both distances exactly \(\sqrt2\). For \(p\le2\), an infinite index set supplies coordinates with norm tending to \(0\), and a unit vector supported on such a coordinate gives both \(p\)-th powers equal to \(1-a^p+(1+a^2)^{p/2}\to2\). For the upper bound, a one-coordinate unit vector reduces every candidate witness to \(1-a^p+(1+a^2)^{p/2}\); the derivative of \((1+a^2)^{p/2}-a^p\) is nonpositive for \(p<2\), zero at \(p=2\), and nonnegative for \(p>2\). This yields exactly \(2^{1/p}\) below \(2\) and \(\sqrt2\) above it. Hypotheses and endpoint \(p=1\) are explicitly covered.

originality.rationale: The closest inspected papers provide qualitative local-octahedrality stability for vector-valued/absolute sums and define the quantitative index \(s(X)\), but the inspected statements do not compute \(s(\ell_p(\Gamma;H))\) for a Hilbert fibre. The theorem gives an exact phase law and, for \(p>2\), a value \(\sqrt2\) that differs from the scalar atomic \(\ell_p\) benchmark. Dedicated semantic searches for the invariant, Hilbert-valued aliases, the exact constant, and equivalent direct-sum language returned no covering scientific record. A residual risk remains that the same infimum-supremum constant has been calculated under a geometric-constant name not surfaced by these searches.
residual_risks: The same infimum-supremum quantity may occur under terminology from the geometric-constants literature not indexed by the searched aliases.
The theorem is not claimed for finite index sets when \(p<2\), so no originality conclusion is made for that adjacent finite-dimensional problem.

value.rationale: This is a natural exact invariant calculation on the canonical vector-valued sequence spaces \(\ell_p(\Gamma;H)\). It isolates a sharp transition at \(p=2\) and a substantive fibre effect: for \(p>2\), adding a two-dimensional Hilbert direction changes the exact local-octahedrality scale from the scalar atomic value \(2^{1/p}\) to \(\sqrt2\). The result therefore supplies a quantitative benchmark for vector-valued octahedrality theory rather than a routine restatement of a qualitative permanence theorem.
